body:
Point 1

> 17.2.1 Verify that the key for the Datagram Transport Layer Security (DTLS) certificate is private by ensuring it is not reused in existing products or open-source projects and confirming it is not distributed or leaked.

By this wording it does not seem like a verifiable thing. Is it covered by general crypto requirements?

---

Point 2

> 17.2.2 Verify that the media server is configured to use and support strong and secure DTLS cipher suites and DTLS-SRTP protection profiles.

Is it anywhere described, what the "strong and secure" is?

---

Point 5

> 17.3.1 Verify that the signalling server is able to continue processing incoming signalling messages during a flood attack. This should be achieved by implementing rate limiting at the signalling level.

Is the point here to "continue processing incoming signalling messages during a flood attack" or "avoid and defend against flood attack"

---

Point 6

> 17.3.2 Verify that the signalling server is able to is able to continue processing signalling messages when encountering malformed signalling messages.

What is the problem to solve here? Does it require a kind of input validation to avoid "malformed signalling messages" being processed?

---

# Solved


Point 3

> 17.2.4 Verify that the media server is able to continue processing incoming media traffic when encountering malformed SRTP packets.

SRTP

---

Point 4

> 17.2.8 Verify that the DTLS certificate is checked against the SDP fingerprint attribute, terminating the media stream if the check fails, to ensure the authenticity of the media stream.

DTLS, SDP

comments.body: ping @randomstuff - you may have a word or two to say about those comments.
ping @sandrogauci as the author of the chapter

> > 17.2.1 Verify that the key for the Datagram Transport Layer Security (DTLS) certificate is private by ensuring it is not reused in existing products or open-source projects and confirming it is not distributed or leaked.
> 
> By this wording it does not seem like a verifiable thing. Is it covered by general crypto requirements?

Yes, maybe it would be enough to rely on 13.3.1 ("[…] Secrets must not be included in application source code or included in build artifacts.").

> > 17.2.2 Verify that the media server is configured to use and support strong and secure DTLS cipher suites and DTLS-SRTP protection profiles.
>
> Is it anywhere described, what the "strong and secure" is?

We should say "uses only approved cryptographic mechanisms" instead of "strong and secure".

For these, I would want to:

* remove these requirements;
* make sure that the generic requirements V11/V12 requirements are worded so that they are applicable to this as well;
* add a note saying something like:
  * "For the DTLS and SRTP communications of WebRTC, the requirements of V11 and V12 are applicable"
  * "For the DTLS and SRTP communications of WebRTC, see the requirements the requirements of V11 and V12."
  * WebRTC rely on DTLS and SRP for secure communications. The requirements of V11 and V12 are applicable to WebRTC DTLS and SRTP communications."

> > 17.3.1 Verify that the signalling server is able to continue processing incoming signalling messages during a flood attack. This should be achieved by implementing rate limiting at the signalling level.
>
> Is the point here to "continue processing incoming signalling messages during a flood attack" or "avoid and defend against flood attack"

I don't know.

Should we say "This can", instead of "This should"?

***

> > 17.3.2 Verify that the signalling server **is able to is able to** continue processing signalling messages when encountering malformed signalling messages.
>
> What is the problem to solve here? Is it requires a kind of input validation to avoid "malformed signalling messages" being processed?

I don't know. And I don't know if this requirement is really needed or if more general requirements are enough?

Moreover, there is a spurious "is able to" 😄

> DTLS, DTLS-SRTP
>
> SRTP
>
> DTLS, SDP

Do you mean we should define those somewhere (in the glossary)?

* **Datagram Transport Layer Security** (DTLS) – A cryptographic protocols that provide communication security over a network connection. It is based on the TLS protocol but adapted for protecting datagram-oriented protocols.
* **DTLS-SRTP** – A mechanism for using a DTLS handshake for establishing key material for a SRTP session. Defined in RFC 5764.
* **Secure Real-time Transport Protocol** (SRTP) and **Secure RTCP** (SRTCP)- A profile of the RTP and RTCP protocols providing support for message encryption, authentication and integrity protection.
* **Session Description Protocol** (SDP) - A message format for setting up multimedia session (used for example in WebRTC).

Other things we might want to add:

* WebRTC
* TURN / STUN
* **Real-time Transport Protocol** (RTP)  and **Real-time Transport Control Protocol** (RTCP) - Two related protocols used for transporting multimedia streams (used for example in WebRTC).

We might as well add in the references of V17:

* RFC 5764 - Datagram Transport Layer Security (DTLS) Extension to Establish Keys for the Secure Real-time Transport Protocol (SRTP

> Do you mean we should define those somewhere (in the glossary)?

As requirements are often read and quoted independently out of the document context, then every requirement need to write the acronyms in full length.

But those must be included in the Glossary as well, I did not check that part myself.

@randomstuff could you do me a favour and suggest a simple PR to address these issues? I don't think we want to start messing with the requirements here too much but mostly focus on clarity and dealing with terminology.

I merged the PR made by @randomstuff - so we got improvements for style and to the Glossary.

Some question are still to solve, I updated the original issue description for that.

I would like to get @sandrogauci's input on these points:

---

> Point 1
> 
> > 17.2.1 Verify that the key for the Datagram Transport Layer Security (DTLS) certificate is private by ensuring it is not reused in existing products or open-source projects and confirming it is not distributed or leaked.
> 
> By this wording it does not seem like a verifiable thing. Is it covered by general crypto requirements?
> 

Agree, it would be tricky to verify this. Maybe it needs to be reworded to focus on the fact that it needs to be generated securely and uniquely.

---

> Point 2
> 
> > 17.2.2 Verify that the media server is configured to use and support strong and secure DTLS cipher suites and DTLS-SRTP protection profiles.
> 
> Is it anywhere described, what the "strong and secure" is?

Are the secure cipher suites the same as regular TLS? Is there a central source of truth for of secure protection profiles?

---

> Point 5
> 
> > 17.3.1 Verify that the signalling server is able to continue processing incoming signalling messages during a flood attack. This should be achieved by implementing rate limiting at the signalling level.
> 
> Is the point here to "continue processing incoming signalling messages during a flood attack" or "avoid and defend against flood attack"

So I feel like this is appropriately specific. In principle we want to defend against a flooding attack but the practical goal is to be able to continue to operate. Not sure I see a need to change anything here.

---

> Point 6
> 
> > 17.3.2 Verify that the signalling server is able to is able to continue processing signalling messages when encountering malformed signalling messages.
> 
> What is the problem to solve here? Does it require a kind of input validation to avoid "malformed signalling messages" being processed?

Is the implication that malformed signalling messages could crash the service leading to a denial of service condition? I think maybe this could be made more specific.

---

> I would like to get [@sandrogauci](https://github.com/sandrogauci)'s input on these points:
> 
> > Point 1
> > > 17.2.1 Verify that the key for the Datagram Transport Layer Security (DTLS) certificate is private by ensuring it is not reused in existing products or open-source projects and confirming it is not distributed or leaked.
> > 
> > 
> > By this wording it does not seem like a verifiable thing. Is it covered by general crypto requirements?

For context: This requirement was inspired by a [HackerOne report](https://hackerone.com/reports/531032) documenting how Slack had implemented a default certificate key from an early version of their WebRTC server.

I agree this requirement doesn't prove such vulnerabilities don't exist. This principle applies broadly in cybersecurity.

> Agree, it would be tricky to verify this. Maybe it needs to be reworded to focus on the fact that it needs to be generated securely and uniquely.

Even securely and uniquely generated certificates can be leaked; therefore, this rewording may not be optimal.

The only reliable solution may be to assess the processes governing private key management.

Therefore, how about:

17.2.1 Verify Datagram Transport Layer Security (DTLS) certificate key privacy by evaluating the processes for key generation, storage, and access control.


> > Point 2
> > > 17.2.2 Verify that the media server is configured to use and support strong and secure DTLS cipher suites and DTLS-SRTP protection profiles.
> > 
> > 
> > Is it anywhere described, what the "strong and secure" is?
> 
> Are the secure cipher suites the same as regular TLS? Is there a central source of truth for of secure protection profiles?

17.2.2 This was briefly discussed previously discussed on https://github.com/OWASP/ASVS/issues/2412#issuecomment-2539209624. It also explains why this requirement was created.

I support replacing "strong and secure" with "uses only approved cryptographic mechanisms," though this remains ambiguous without referencing specific standards like NIST SP 800‑52 Rev. 2 or BSI TR‑02102‑2 (Version 2025‑01).

Suggested text:

17.2.2 Verify that the media server implements only current, industry-approved DTLS versions, cipher suites, and DTLS-SRTP protection profiles.

> > Point 5
> > > 17.3.1 Verify that the signalling server is able to continue processing incoming signalling messages during a flood attack. This should be achieved by implementing rate limiting at the signalling level.
> > 
> > 
> > Is the point here to "continue processing incoming signalling messages during a flood attack" or "avoid and defend against flood attack"
> 
> So I feel like this is appropriately specific. In principle we want to defend against a flooding attack but the practical goal is to be able to continue to operate. Not sure I see a need to change anything here.

We were specific in this requirement to clarify our intention. We've observed cases where protection mechanisms ironically caused Denial of Service by preventing the signaling server from processing legitimate messages. We can amend the wording to include "legitimate" for further clarity.

> > Point 6
> > > 17.3.2 Verify that the signalling server is able to is able to continue processing signalling messages when encountering malformed signalling messages.
> > 
> > 
> > What is the problem to solve here? Does it require a kind of input validation to avoid "malformed signalling messages" being processed?
> 
> Is the implication that malformed signalling messages could crash the service leading to a denial of service condition? I think maybe this could be made more specific.

Crashes aren't specifically mentioned because improperly handled malformed signaling messages can cause denial of service even without server crashes.

> 17.2.1 Verify that the key for the Datagram Transport Layer Security (DTLS) certificate is private by ensuring it is not reused in existing products or open-source projects and confirming it is not distributed or leaked.

Proving that the private key is not leaked is not possible but we can verify that the key is not hardcoded in the application at the very least.

> Are the secure cipher suites the same as regular TLS?

Yes, the ciphersuites are shared with TLS and we can use the same list (or criterions) of allowed ciphersuites.

> Is there a central source of truth for of secure protection profiles?

There are guidelines such as:

* [ciphersuite.info](https://ciphersuite.info/)
* [Mozilla SSL Configuration Generator](https://ssl-config.mozilla.org/)

And we have list of allowed encryption methods, MACs, hashing methods in the appendix and the reader can derive a list of allowed ciphersuites from that. I'm not sure I want to maintain a list of ciphersuites (dans SRTP protection profiles) in the appendix however. Ideally we could derive it from the list of underlying approved cryptographic mechanisms using a script.

@elarlang what are your comments on this, especially taking into account the previous discussions.

@sandrogauci thanks!

> [@elarlang](https://github.com/elarlang) what are your comments on this, especially taking into account the previous discussions.

I shared my concerns, and I don't think I have anything to add. Concerns were also more about how to organize and validate the requirement in ASVS, not about technical details.

I'm looking more towards @randomstuff - he has enough knowledge technically to solve it, and also understands what we expect from a requirement in the ASVS.
